transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Well, what brings me in is... I just keep forgetting things that I really shouldn't. It's getting pretty frustrating. 

Like, I'll completely forget about my heart follow-up appointments, or I'll forget to call the clinic back when I'm supposed to. Even just doing regular things, I'll show up to do a repair job and realize I didn't even bring the right tools with me. I just can't seem to keep these things straight in my head lately.
Did these difficulties with your memory develop gradually over time, or did they seem to start suddenly?

Well, I'd say it's tied to a specific event, really. It's been causing real trouble for about a year and two months now. 

That was right around the time I had a cardiac scare. After that happened, I was forced to cut way back on all the walking and the projects I was doing. Those things always used to keep me settled, you know? But once I couldn't do all that moving around anymore, that's when I really started losing track of things.
Looking back to your childhood or school years, did you ever have trouble with restlessness, paying attention, or staying organized?

Yeah, I did. Even as a boy in grade school, I was the kid who just couldn't stay in his seat. I'd always blurt out answers in class, and, well... I got a lot of notes sent home to my parents for talking too much. So the restlessness has always been there, I guess.

latest_inference.note: Lifelong history of hyperactive, impulsive, and restless behavior starting in grade school confirms childhood onset of ADHD, unmasked in adulthood when physical coping mechanisms decreased; rules out primary adult-onset neurocognitive or mood disorders like F01, F06.7, and F32.

inference_history.note: Initial differential for new-onset forgetfulness and executive/memory difficulties includes neurocognitive disorders (Alzheimer's, vascular, or unspecified dementia, mild cognitive disorder), pseudodementia/depression, and adult attention-deficit disorder.
